more.text: Configuration drift and manual CLI work are the problems it targets.

sides.text: Management plane: configure and monitor. Control plane: routing decisions. Data plane: forwarding

Data (forwarding) plane: normal user traffic forwarded through the device
Control plane: decisions about how to forward traffic (e.g. routing protocol/STP updates)
Management plane: how the device itself is configured and monitored (CLI, GUI, SNMP, API)

more.text: In a traditional model, all three run independently, decentralised, on every device.

sides.text: Traditional: each device has its own control plane. Controller-based: a central controller programs devices

more.text: Gives a single policy and automation point.

sides.text: Centralises control-plane functions in a controller, while data-plane functions stay decentralised since they need specialised hardware (ASICs, TCAM) on each device

more.text: The controller talks to network devices via a Southbound Interface (SBI) and to administrators/automation software via a Northbound Interface (NBI).

sides.text: SDN adds a fourth plane: applications that talk to the controller via its NBI

more.text: When a configuration change is requested, the controller decides how to implement it and pushes changes to devices via SBI.

sides.text:
OpenPK: Cisco-proprietary API using Java, C or Python
OpenFlow: imperative SDN model, sends detailed instructions to devices
OpFlex: declarative SDN model, sends intent and leaves implementation to devices
NETCONF: open standard using XML and RPC, usually over SSH
RESTCONF: open standard using JSON/XML and REST, usually over HTTPS

REST, using JSON over HTTP (usually)
Open Society Gateway initiative (OSGi), Java-based
Open SDN is a model from the Open Networking Foundation, centred on the OpenFlow SBI

more.text: OpenDaylight (ODL) is the most popular Open SDN controller — open-source, maintained by The Linux Foundation, supporting other SBIs beyond OpenFlow, with an OSGi Java API and REST API for NBI.

sides.text: Application Centric Infrastructure — an intent-based, data-centre-focused SDA model using a spine-leaf topology (all spine switches connect to all leaf switches, but no spine-spine or leaf-leaf links)

more.text: Controlled by an Application Policy Infrastructure Controller (APIC), which translates administrator-defined Endpoint Group (EPG) policies into device configuration pushed via OpFlex.

sides.text: A now-discontinued Cisco controller that enabled SDN for devices without specialised SBI support, using existing tools (Telnet/SSH, SNMP) instead

more.text: Left the control plane untouched, focusing on management-plane functions. Its features have mostly been folded into Cisco DNA Center (DNAC).

sides.text: An SDA model for enterprise campuses, made of a physical underlay (devices, cabling, wireless links) and a logical overlay carried over VXLAN tunnels

more.text: A greenfield deployment builds an all-new underlay; a brownfield deployment reuses existing infrastructure, requiring care over device compatibility.

sides.text: In greenfield deployments, switch-to-switch traffic is fully routed (Layer 3) rather than switched (Layer 2), typically using IS-IS

more.text: This removes the need for Spanning Tree, since a routed underlay avoids Layer 2 loops without blocking any links.

sides.text: SDA Edge Nodes and Control Node
SDA Edge Nodes are Layer 3 switches replacing traditional access switches, acting as the default gateway for endpoints (making FHRP unnecessary)

more.text: The SDA Control Node is a LISP map server: when a packet arrives, its Edge Node looks up the destination's Endpoint Identifier at the Control Node, which returns the Routing Locator (RLOC) of the correct egress Edge Node.

sides.text: Switches that connect the SDA fabric to endpoints beyond its control, usually WAN routers
The controller for an SDA network — controls both underlay and overlay in greenfield deployments, but only the overlay when the underlay is pre-existing and manually configured

more.text: Uses a REST API for NBI, and SSH/Telnet (legacy devices) or RESTCONF/NETCONF (SDA-native devices) for SBI.

sides.text: Replaces traditional ACLs with policies based on Scalable Group Tags (SGTs): administrators define endpoint groups and set which group can communicate with which other group

more.text: Greatly simplifies access security management compared to traditional ACLs in large deployments.

sides.text: Underlay: the physical IP network. Overlay: virtual tunnels (VXLAN) on top. Fabric: both together

more.text: SD-Access uses LISP for control and VXLAN for data.

sides.text: As networks grow, small untracked changes cause configuration drift — divergence between individual devices and the approved reference configuration

more.text: Configuration management tools solve this via centralised config provisioning (templates + variables, validated before upload) and monitoring/enforcement of divergence.

sides.text: A push-model, agentless tool written in Python — it doesn't rely on software running on target devices, but logs in itself via SSH or NETCONF to make changes

more.text: Configuration consists of Playbooks (actions to take), an Inventory (devices, grouped, with variables), Templates (for config files) and Variables (fed into templates).

sides.text: A pull-model, agent-based tool written in Ruby — an agent on the device connects to the Puppet Master to report changes and check for updates

more.text: Devices without agent support can use a proxy agent connecting via SSH. Communicates over HTTPS port 8140. Configuration centres on declarative Manifest files, backed by Resources, Classes and Modules.

sides.text: Similar to Puppet — pull-model, agent-based, written in Ruby, communicating over HTTPS port 443

more.text: Can also run standalone using cookbooks stored locally or in a .tar.gz archive. Its components are Recipes (gathered into Cookbooks) and Runlists (which recipe applies to which host).
